titleStmt.title: Building Comfortability and Computation Schedulability: A Comparative Study

analytic.title: Building Comfortability and Computation Schedulability: A Comparative Study

div.p: Many energy consuming devices, especially thermostatically controlled electrical devices (TCED) such as airconditioners, room heaters and refrigerators, have a periodic execution profile, tempting us to draw an analogy between the allocation of electrical power to TCEDs vis-à-vis the allocation of CPU time to computational tasks. The resulting mapping naturally leads us to make use of traditional real-time scheduling policies such as earliest deadline first (EDF) and least slacktime first (LSF) (and the associated schedulability analysis) in managing TCEDs to deal with energy management and peak power constraints. However, the analogy is not without detractors: the execution time (interval when a TCED is ON) and the period of a TCED are dynamic. In this work, we critically examine the similarities and the differences between real-time tasks and TCED activities. The focus of this work is to analyze the ability of scheduling policies from the real-time domain to attain desired thermal comfort within designated spaces, which we term as comfortability.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recent research suggests modeling of household electrical devices as periodically activated tasks and application of real-time analysis techniques to schedule them [1][2] [3]. The motivation behind this is the reduction in peak demand through coordinated scheduling of household appliances. This is because i) peak energy consumption has an impact on upfront capital costs and hence on energy tariffs and ii) a smoother load profile improves grid stability and quality of service (less occurrences of blackouts, brownouts & load shedding). The largest contributors to energy consumptions in a building (residential and commercial) are thermostat controlled electrical devices (TCED or TCE devices) like airconditioners, refrigerators and room heaters. These devices do not run continuously, but have a periodic ON-OFF execution profile, as shown in Figure 1, which depicts the operating characteristics of an AC generated from experimental data. When a TCED is ON it consumes electrical power, which is analogous to a computational task consuming CPU time. We refer to the time duration for which a TCED remains ON and the duration for which it remains OFF within its duty cycle as the ON-time and the OFF-time of the TCED respectively. As shown in Figure 1, the ON-time and an OFFtime of a TCED within its duty cycle are equivalent to the execution time C i and laxity L i respectively; the duty-cycle hence is analogous to period P i = C i + L i . div.p: Fig. 1. AC as a periodic task real-time system community to draw an analogy between the allocation of electrical power to TCEDs vis-à-vis the allocation of CPU time to computational tasks. The resulting mapping naturally leads us to make use of traditional realtime scheduling policies such as earliest deadline first (EDF), least slack-time first (LSF) (and the associated schedulability analysis) [4] etc. in managing TCEDs to deal with energy management and peak power constraints. However, the major difference between a computational task and a TCED task is that in case of a computational task, preemption has no effect on its execution time or period. But, in case of a TCED task, its execution time C i and the period P i are dynamic and depends on when it is preempted [5]. The limitation of traditional realtime scheduling policies in scheduling TCE devices is also pointed out in [6] as their applicability is restricted to tasks whose worst case response time is known a priori. It motivated us to critically examine the similarities and the differences between real-time tasks and TCED activities. We find that though there are similarities between them, dissimilarities are also many. This restricts the applicability of traditional real-time policies in coordinated scheduling of TCEDs for reduction in peak demand without compromising thermal comfort. The focus of this work is to analyze the ability of scheduling policies from the real-time domain to attain desired thermal comfort within designated spaces, which we term as comfortability.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section II, the similarities and difference between real-time task and TCED task is discussed. Section III discusses limitations of traditional real-time policies in scheduling TCE devices. Related work is discussed in Section IV followed by the conclusion.

div.head: II. REAL-TIME TASK VS TCED TASK
div.p: In this section, we identify the key differences between real-time task scheduling and the power allocation to TCEDs. We take the example of a system of n AC units maintaining the temperature of n thermally de-coupled zones. It may be noted here that all thermostatically controlled devices like AC, refrigerator and heater maintains the temperature of its zone within a band, usually within ±1 0 C of its set temperature. We refer to the temperature-band within which the zone temperature T i is maintained by a TCED as comfort-band or CB [T L , T U ]. We assume that a centralized controller replaces individual thermostat controllers of the ACs and maintains temperatures of the the n zones within the desired CB.

First, let us re-visit the functioning of a typical feedback controller. As shown in Figure 2, the main components of a feedback control loop are i) sensor & sampler, ii) controller and ii) actuator. The sensor output, which provides the plant state variable (temperature T i in our case) is sampled at a particular frequency. The controller either i) polls the sampler periodically or ii) gets an interrupt when the sample is ready. After receiving the state variable, the controller starts computation (e.g., execution of control logic/interlocks or processing of some special control technique say, Kalman Filter) and sends output to the actuator. The job of the controller is to complete the computation within a given time after it receives the sample, so that the plant state variable does not deviate from its set point to an unacceptable value within that period. After appropriate control analysis, the value of the real-time task period P i is chosen from the suitable sample frequency. So far as the computation-time is concerned, the design requirement of a controller are as follows.
• The controller shall complete the execution of computation task on or before the next sampling time, which defines the deadline D i (≤ P i ).

• The controller shall schedule the computation tasks such a way that each task completes execution before its deadline. TCE devices, a special class of cyber physical electrical systems modeled as real-time tasks, are different from the traditional controller tasks we discussed. This is because a TCED task actually models the plant, which is AC in our case.

Note that the time an AC takes to bring down the temperature from T U to T L becomes its execution time C i and the time for the zone temperature to rise from T L to T U , when the AC is off, becomes its laxity L i .

In order to differentiate between the two, we refer to the traditional controller tasks as computational task and the other ones as TCED tasks. The two fundamental differences between a computational task and a TCED task are as follows.

• When a computational task executes, the plant state variable does not change. To be precise, control requirement demands that the computation task execution time should be too short to cause any significant change in the plant state variable. In contrast, when a TCED task executes, it keeps on changing the state variable. • The worst case execution time (WCET) of a computation task is time invariant, i.e., the CPU-time requirement of a computational task has no dependency on when CPU is given to it, within its period. In contrast, a TCED task does not bring uniform change in state variable per unit time of its execution due to the exponential nature of its thermal characteristics [Figure 1]. Therefore, the energyrequirement of a TCED varies based on when1 power is given to it, within its duty-cycle. It also makes the execution time C i and period P i dynamic when a TCED task is preempted [5]. How the exponential thermal characteristics and the dynamic C i and P i of a TCED task affects comfort-band is discussed in Section III-C. Table I summarizes the similarities and the differences between real-time computational tasks and TCED tasks.

We observe that the modeling of electrical devices as realtime tasks, in effect, attempts to do away with the sensorsampler feedback in the control loop. The controller simply needs to keeps track of the ON-time and period of the TCEDs as shown in Figure 3. Note that the controller needs no feedback as the ON-OFF commands to TCEDs are sent by itself and therefore, it can keep track of the execution time of TCED tasks. The logic behind it is that once the periodic operation of a TCED within a particular comfort-band [T L , T U ] is modeled as a real-time task, it is expected that there is no need for temperature feedback, so long as the feasibility analysis guarantees execution of every TCED task within its deadline and they are scheduled according to the applicable policy.

It may be noted here that if the zone temperatures are not maintained simply by scheduling TCED tasks, then we will need a master controller on top of the TCED task scheduler. The master controller may take feedback of the plant state variable and modify the TCED task parameters like priority, worst-case execution time etc. By doing so, it should be possible to maintain the desired zone temperature by scheduling the TCED tasks according to the adopted policy from the real-time domain. But, it calls for an analysis on how environmental parameter feedback can be accounted for in schedulability analysis.

div.head: A. Peak Demand Constraint and TCED task
div.p: The idea behind modeling TCE devices as real-time tasks originated from the need for reduction in peak demand [1] by applying real-time scheduling policies in controlling them. But, traditional controller in a control loop is not concerned with the electrical power requirement of plant equipment like air-conditioner as mentioned in Table I. Its only concern is to maintain zone temperature within the desired comfort-band [T L , T U ]. So, we focus mainly on the schedulability of TCED task in the context of peak demand constraint.

div.head: III. REAL-TIME POLICIES AND TCED SCHEDULING
div.p: In this section, we discuss how and why real-time scheduling policies can fail in scheduling TCE devices for maintaining comfortability in building. We find that restart-delay requirement of TCED as well as maintenance of comfort-band of the zones may not be guaranteed by traditional real-time scheduling techniques.

div.head: A. System Model
div.p: We consider a system of n ACs installed in a building. But, peak power demand constraint allows only m out of n ACs to run at a time. ACs can be considered as a representative TCED, because all these devices work under the same basic principle of heat-transfer [7]. So, analysis carried out on AC system will also be valid for heating and refrigeration system.

div.head: B. Restart Delay Constraint
div.p: Restart delay is an important requirement in scheduling TCE devices like air-conditioners and refrigerators. A delay of about 3 minutes is mandatory before a compressor driven TCE device can be switched on again once it is switched off. This delay allows the pressures in the system to equalize so that the compressor does not start under a load. If restart-delay is not provided, the compressor may not start due to an overload or it can even damage the equipment. But in traditional real-time scheduling policies there is no notion of restart-delay. Once a task is preempted, it can be restarted the moment it receives CPU-time. Here, with the help of an example we discuss the analbetween computational task scheduling and coordinated scheduling of TCE devices. Further, we show how real-time task scheduling violates the requirement of mandatory restartdelay.

Coordinated scheduling of n TCEDs with available power for m TCEDs is analogous to scheduling n tasks on m processors. Therefore, for TCE devices, application of global EDF [8] scheduling comes as a natural choice as it deals with schedulability of n tasks on m uniform processors. We divide the available power into m logical power sources and schedule the allocation of power to n TCE devices. With the help of a simple example, we now compare multiprocessor task scheduling with scheduling of power-allocation to TCEDs. We take a system of two real-time tasks τ 1 (7, 5) and τ 2 (4, 3), which are scheduled on two processor as shown in Figure 4a. It may be noted that a task is represented here as τ i (P i , C i ), where C i is the execution time and P i is its period. D 1 (7,5) and D 2 (4, 3) are two TCE devices, where D 1 runs for 5 units of time and D 2 runs for 3 units of time within their respective duty-cycle of 7 and 4 units of time. We assume that power required to run both these devices are available. We logically divide the power requirement of D 1 and D 2 into two separate power sources. It can be observed from Figure 4b that scheduling of D 1 (7, 5) and D 2 (4, 3) on two separate logical power sources are exactly similar to scheduling of two tasks τ 1 (7, 5) and τ 2 (4, 3) in 2 CPUs, as shown in Figure 4a. Now, assume that another task τ 3 (7, 3) is to be scheduled using the same 2 processors. A feasible schedule can be produced using Global EDF scheduler as shown in Figure 5.

But, if we are to allocate power to an additional TCE device D 3 (7, 3), which needs power for 3 units of time in its dutycycle of 7 units, a similar schedule will not be feasible. This is because, as it can be observed from Figure 5, the restart-delay requirement of task τ 2 (analogous to TCED D 2 ) is violated at time t = 8.

2) Existing Techniques to Accommodate Restart-Delay: In order to ensure restart-delay t R in a TCE device, it is required that once powered off at time t, it will not be powered on till t + t R . Considering restart-delay in a real-time task model is equivalent to introducing it as a constraint in scheduability analysis. Now, we discuss available options to handle restartdelay constraint using existing art.

• Option I: Existing technique handles precedence constraint [4] by increasing the worst-case execution time (WCET) of the constrained task commensurate to the time it can be blocked due to the constraint (restartdelay). This is not workable, because modified WCET accommodates a delay equivalent to t R in schedulability analysis, but does not ensure specific delay between completion of execution and the next start-time of a task. • Option II: Use option I and do the schedulability analysis.

But, let a master scheduler change (lower) the priority of the task if it is time for it to get CPU-time (according to priority assignment by the adopted policy) but t R -time is not elapsed after its preemption. We find that Option II is feasible but not a practical solution. This is because, restart-delay of about 3 minutes in a typical execution time of 15 to 30 minutes of a TCED is quite significant. Therefore, increasing WCET of each TCED task by t R will result in too pessimistic outcome of schedulability analysis to implement it effectively in real-life applications. Figure 6 shows scheduling of 4 ACs under global EDF policy (discussed in Section III-C). It can be observed from Figure 6 that during 2 hours of coordinated scheduling of 3 out of 4 TCEDs, the need for imposing restart-delay constraint came only four times; 2 times during the time period between 50 to 60 minutes and once each at about 86 and 116 minutes. So, it goes against the idea of including restart-delay within WCET.

The following example further illustrates the practical limitations of option II. We carried out feasibility analysis for various combinations of 4 ACs from a set of two types of ACs having different thermal characteristics as follows. τ 1 (P i , C i ) = {τ 1 (28, 9.8), τ 2 (36.1, 19.1)}, where P i and C i denotes period and execution time respectively. The comparison is carried out between the global EDF [8] and our recent work on TCBM [5] schedulability analysis. TCBM is chosen because, it represents schedulability of TCE devices based on environment parameter feedback. The schedulability criterion is reproduced here from [5] for the sake of completeness.

Theorem 1: If peak-demand constraint allows m out n ACs to run at a time and ACs are scheduled by the TCBM algorithm, all the zone temperatures will eventually fall from the ambient T a to a value T i (T L ≤ T i < T U ) and the CB [T L , T U ] will be maintained thereafter, if the following condition is satisfied.
div.formula: m i=1 abs(S i f (T i )) > n-m i=1 S i r (T i )(1)
div.p: where, i) S i f (T i ) and S i r (T i ) represent the slopes of the cooling curve and the warming curve of AC i respectively, ii) the sum on the left is obtained from the first m of the n ACs arranged in ascending order of their cooling-slopes, and iii) the sum on the right is obtained from the first (n -m) of the n ACs arranged in descending order of their warming-slopes.

The summary of the results are shown in Table II. It can be observed from Table II that when restart delay is taken into consideration, global EDF schedulability analysis comes out with positive results only in case of one out of the five combinations of ACs.

Therefore, we conclude that it is not advisable to model TCE devices as real-time task, because existing technique from real-time domain is highly pessimistic in handling restartdelay, a mandatory requirement for TCED operation.

div.head: C. Violation of comfort-band
div.p: We take a the case 4 ACs and assume that under peak demand constraint power is available only for 3 ACs at a time. This set of 4 ACs α = {α i | i = 1, 2, • • • , 4} are modeled as periodic tasks according to their ON-time and OFF-time duration in their duty-cycles. The AC task set obtained by curve-fitting from experimental data of their thermal profile are as follows. We applied global EDF schedulability criterion [8] for scheduling the above 4 tasks on 3 processors and found them schedulable. The resulting schedule for 2 hours is shown in Figure 6. It can be observed from Figure 6 that comfort-band is violated by AC3 (α 3 ) at t = 26 minute, at t = 85 minute and later. Also, it can be seen from Figure 6 that comfort-bands of the respective zones are also violated by AC2 & AC4. It happened because, going by the scheduling policy, the global EDF scheduler did not give CPU to α 3 (AC3) as it did not have the earliest deadline at the time instants t = 26 and t = 85 minutes. The comfort-bands would not have been violated by an AC if the scheduling policy allowed preemption of some other AC whose zone temperature was Fig. 6. Scheduling 4 ACs with available power for 3 ACs using global EDF policy below T U , the upper limit of the comfort-band. For example, the comfort-band of the zone controlled by AC3 would not have been violated at t = 85 minute, if the scheduling policy allowed preemption of either AC2 or AC4, whose zone temperature were well below T U , to make power available to AC3. Therefore, it can be concluded that even though the task set α is schedulable according to some real-time scheduling policy, comfort-band can be violated, because such scheduling policies do not consider environmental parameter feed back in making scheduling decisions.

In order to take care of comfort-band violation, we need to introduce a master controller on top of the TCED task scheduler, which will act based on the feedback of the plant state variable (temperature). Under this scheme, the scheduler will schedule n tasks on m processor according to EDF policy provided plant state variable allows it. If the plant state variable associated to a particular zone goes beyond comfort-band, its priority will be enhanced by the master controller so that the scheduler gives CPU-time by means of preempting some other task having lower priority. Existing art suggests taking care of preemption cost by adding it up to the worst-case execution time and carry out the schedulability analysis. But, the following issues still remains to be resolved. Unresolved Issues:

• Finding means to quantify the maximum number of preemption that can occur in a cycle due to the possible violations in the comfort-band. (in case of a master controller taking corrective action) • Increased TCED switching due to additional switching caused by scheduling policy itself. (E.g., unnecessary switching of AC4 during 40 -60 min. in Figure 6) • Taking into account of restart-delay on every preemption (switching-off) of a TCE device. It can be impractical to do so as discussed in Section III.

In summary, it can be concluded that though TCEDs exhibits periodic operation, modeling them as real-time task and applying traditional scheduling policies do not guarantee maintenance of building comfortability. Further, result of the schedulability analysis can be unrealistic in handling constraint requirements of real-life implementations [Table II] .

IV. RELATED WORK Modeling the electrical loads as real-time task was first introduced in [1] and the authors suggested use of traditional real-time scheduling algorithms. Similar suggestion is also made in [2]. But, the basic assumption in their work is that the energy consumption characteristics of all electrical loads are linear. But, it is exponential for thermostatically controlled electrical loads like air-conditioners and refrigerators as discussed in our work. Jitter compensation in real-time control system is discussed in [9] which deals with the problem of jitter in real-time control. It is similar to the problem of preemption in TCED control. In their work, the suggested technique is providing compensation to controller that maintains controlled variable to the set (desired) value. But, in our case, the controlled variable (temperature) is maintained within a band. That traditional real-time scheduling algorithms are not suitable for TCED scheduling is also pointed out in [5] and [6]. In [6], the authors argued against it because worstcase execution time is not known a-priori for TCE devices. In this work, we carried out detailed and critical study on the schedulability of real-time tasks and TCE devices.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We discussed modeling of thermostatically controlled electrical devices as real-time tasks and critically examined the limitations of traditional real-time policies like EDF and LSF in scheduling TCE devices. We discussed similarities & differences between scheduling n tasks on m uniform multiprocessor and scheduling m out of n TCE devices under peak demand constraint. We also established the limitations of traditional algorithms from real-time domain in scheduling TCE devices and thereby attempted to highlight the unresolved issues discussed in Section III, which needs further research.
